==Problem==
The sequence <imath>1,x,y,z</imath> is arithmetic. The sequence <imath>1,p,q,z</imath> is geometric. Both sequences are strictly increasing and contain only integers, and <imath>z</imath> is as small as possible. What is the value of <imath>x+y+z+p+q</imath>?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 66 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 91 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 103 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 132 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 149</imath>

==Solution 1==
Since the geometric sequence is more restrictive, we can test values for the common ratio until we find one that works. After a few tests, we find that a common ratio of <imath>4</imath> results in the geometric sequence <imath>1,4,16,64,</imath> so the arithmetic sequence is <imath>1,22,43,64.</imath> The answer is <imath>4+16+64+22+43=\boxed{\text{(E) }149}.</imath>

A more generalized solution is as follows. 
Let the common difference of the arithmetic sequence be <imath>d</imath>, and the common ratio of the geometric sequence be <imath>r.</imath> Hence, the two sequences are <imath>1,1+d,1+2d,1+3d</imath> and <imath>1,r,r^2,r^3.</imath> Since <imath>z=1+3d=r^3,</imath> the arithmetic sequence is <imath>1,1+d,1+2d,r^3.</imath> Since <imath>d=\dfrac{1+3d-1}{3}=\dfrac{r^3-1}{3}</imath> is a positive integer, we seek the smallest <imath>r\neq1</imath> such that <imath>r^3-1=(r-1)(r^2+r+1)</imath> is divisible by <imath>3,</imath> so the smallest <imath>r</imath> is <imath>4</imath>. The rest follows like above.

~Tacos_are_yummy_1

==Solution 2==

Since <imath>1, x, y, z</imath> is an arithmetic sequence, we have <imath>y = 2x - 1</imath> and <imath>z = 3x - 2</imath>.
Since <imath>1, p, q, z</imath> is a geometric sequence, we have <imath>q = p^2</imath> and <imath>z = p^3</imath>.
Thus <imath>p^3 = 3x - 2.</imath>

Because <imath>p^3 \equiv p \pmod{3}</imath>, we get <imath>3x - 2 \equiv p \pmod{3}</imath>, so <imath>p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}</imath>.
The smallest integer <imath>p > 1</imath> satisfying this is <imath>p = 4</imath>.

Then <imath>64 = 3x - 2</imath> → <imath>x = 22</imath>, <imath>y = 43</imath>, <imath>z = 64</imath>, <imath>q = 16</imath>.
Therefore, <imath>x + y + z + p + q = 22 + 43 + 64 + 4 + 16 = \boxed{\text{(E) }149}</imath>.

~Continuous_Pi

~<imath>\LaTeX</imath> by stevens0209

==Solution 3 (Satisfying and Simple)==

So we have that the arithmetic sequence is <imath>1, x, 2x-1, 3x-2</imath> since
common difference is <imath>x - 1</imath>.

Similarly, geometric sequence is <imath>1, p, p^2, p^3</imath>

So <imath>p^3 = 3x-2</imath>. We test values above 1 (increasing sequence)

We see that <imath>p = 4, x = 22</imath> so our answer is <imath>22 + 43 + 64 + 4 + 16 = \boxed{149}</imath>

~Aarav22

==Solution 4 (Easy to identify)==

Since only integer ratios work for the geometric series, test the ratio of <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, and <imath>4</imath>, by having <imath>z</imath> be <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, and <imath>4</imath> cubed, and finding that <imath>\frac{64-1}{3}=21</imath> (since that is the common ratio of the arithmetic sequence to get <imath>64</imath> from <imath>1</imath> in <imath>4</imath> terms), then <imath>22+43+4+16+64=149</imath>, which is E.

Note: We divide <imath>z</imath> by <imath>3</imath> because to get from <imath>p</imath> to <imath>z</imath> you have to add <imath>3d</imath> which is the difference of the arithmetic sum.

-Amon26(note)
==Solution 5 (Ratio)==

We have <imath>1, x, y, z</imath> as an arithmetic sequence. If we let <imath>d</imath> be the rate of change, <imath>z - y = d</imath>, <imath>y - x = d</imath> and <imath>x - 1 = d</imath>, now you could follow with solution 3, or, you could just have the geometric sequence ratio be <imath>r</imath>, so we have <imath>\frac{z}{q} = r</imath>, <imath>\frac{q}{p} = r</imath>, <imath>\frac{p}{1} = r</imath>.

Wait, we see <imath>\frac{p}{1} = r</imath>, so <imath>p = r</imath>, then <imath>q = p^2</imath>, then <imath>p^3 = z</imath>, and since these have to be integers, we have to get a value <imath>p</imath> that works as an integer for the arithmetic sequence.

Because we add our common difference <imath>d</imath> 3 times, we see that <imath>(p^3-1)/3=d</imath> where d is an integer (this is because if we try 3 we get <imath>z = p</imath> which violates <imath>p^3 = z</imath>, where <imath>p = 3</imath>, however, the starting is one, so we find a value that when subtracted by 1, gets us a multiple of 3 so the arithmetic sequence works) and we find a value <imath>p = 4</imath>.

The arithmetic sequence is <imath>1, 22, 43, 64</imath>, where <imath>21 = d</imath> and it follows as <imath>p^3 - 1 = 63 = 3d</imath>, and adding it up we get 129 for the arithmetic and since 64 is already <imath>z</imath> so we only need to add <imath>p</imath> and <imath>q</imath> or <imath>p^2</imath>, we would get 20 and <imath>20 + 129 = \boxed{\textbf{(E) } 149}</imath>.

- Randomuser456
